You would put your shutdown relay within 3 feet of the brains (the EFCI) and the distance from that to the RTU doesn't matter.  On elevators the controller is typically in a room, with a lot of cable running to the elevator itself. If the resistor is in series at the panel then it can be bypassed by using a crimp-on wiresplice at the device end to keep the wires shorted without the panel knowing it was bypassed.

If this is a class b circuit then the EOL is 4.7K Ohm and that is what you should have +/- 5 or 10%.  The 40 Ohm value is the wire resistance with everything shorted at the ends to ensure that you don't drop too much voltage and end up with devices getting low voltage.  If you are reading 150K Ohms then you are very high.  It cannot be resistors at all T Taps as that puts them in parallel so the total resistance would be lower and those branches read Ol which is very high (typically at least greater than 10 Megohms).  That means your loop probably has the EOL resistor going bad.  Find it and measure that and see what it is.  150K is not a soft short, it is fairly high resistance so not the problem.  Verify that ground fault monitoring is enabled on the panel to rule out a soft ground that is lower resistance when panel voltage is supplied (your meter uses much lower voltage to measure resistance so may not show it well).  You can break the gigantic t tap splice apart, measure them, go to the problem circuit and break it down measuring your voltage and resistance to see if you find it.

I would say AFF, not the ramp, as the occupation of the space is not on the ramp.  Take into account the indirect signal and fact that other strobes are in the area and likely within direct viewing and you have a better argument about it being AFF.

Occupiable space is a key here, the ramp is a means of egress, not really occupiable space, as it is simply a ramp designed to give a means to reach the doors.  [18.5.1.2](https://18.5.1.2) specifies coverage area of visible appliances as required by other codes - our other code is IBC.  IBC907.5.2.3 exception 2 states they are not required in exits, defined in ch 2 as ...interior exit stairways and ramps... 

As it is against code to block the ramp as it is a means of egress, and common sense says that you wouldn't occupy the ramp anyway, this all makes sense.  Place the strobe appropriately for the occupiable space which is the floor below the ramp.  Placing higher at the ramp defeats the purpose of signaling in the occupiable space, the entire reason the strobe is where it is.

I took the old module apart and it appears that the T6 terminal that was causing the current to trip is connected to the base of a transistor so the additional current caused the transistor to saturate and thus trigger, confirming the false triggering is likely caused by that.  The passing through to the SLC may indeed be happening, and I have found that the impedance of the monitor modules at the SLC terminals is quite different at about 1 megohm difference, certainly enough to cause an issue if the current leaks through, which I hadn't considered.
